newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK stocks put rates behind, focus on handover.
newsitem.headline: HK stocks put rates behind, focus on handover.

text.p: Hong Kong stock investors have put interest rate fears behind them for the time being and are now focusing on post-handover plays in the run up to Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule, analysts said on Wednesday.
"The interest rate thing is still on hold and it has been in the background of this market for the last year," said Howard Gorges, a director at South China Brokerage.
"But the China picture is the more positive thing that is coming forward now and we also have the handover," he said.

The U.S. Federal Reserve voted on Tuesday to leave interest rates unchanged, prompting a rally in Hong Kong's blue chips to new record highs. The Hang Seng Index surged 162.35 points to a record high of 14,398.55 on Wednesday before easing later to end the day down 0.68 point at 14,235.52.
"The next (Federal Reserve) meeting is in July and will certainly give the market some breathing space," said Grant Forster, vice president at BT Fund Managers.

"If the level of political tensions (in Hong Kong) remains as it is, which is quite low, and the interest rate environment remains benign, then I don't think there is any reason to pull back significantly."
China plays have already been a dominant theme in the Hong Kong stock market as the territory prepares to revert to Chinese control on July 1.

The feeding frenzy for China-related stocks reached fever pitch this week with the launch of Beijing Enterprises Holdings Ltd's initial public offering. The share issue has drawn unprecedented demand from investors in Hong Kong.
"People are generally optimistic about China because the outlook for the economy is quite promising," said Andrew Fernow, director of research at Vickers Ballas.
"Given that the economic outlook in the region is not so promising, the China plays are really what investors are aiming for right now," he said.
Fernow said investors would be looking for companies which would benefit from the policies which the new Special Administrative Region government was likely to implement after the handover.
Certain property companies would benefit from new policies to address a housing shortage in Hong Kong and a commitment to infrastructure development would help others, he said.
Fernow named Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd, Cheung Kong Infrastructure Holdings Ltd, HKR International Ltd and New World Infrastructure Ltd.

"The property companies are going to find more land being made available. That probably means that they might have to share the cake with some of the bigger China companies like China Overseas Land and China Resources," added Gorges.
"We may see more China-controlled entities beginning to participate more in our property market," he said.

Fernow said banks like Bank of East Asia Ltd could benefit from developments in the banking sector "particularly when one sees the need for China to modernise its banking system and open up its banking business."
Liquidity flows from the mainland were also expected to continue in the runup to the handover, helping the market reach new peaks, analysts said.
"Obviously the factor at the moment is the China money coming in," said Robert Rountree, regional strategist at Nomura Research Institute.
"I suspect that the China enthusiasm will only intensify so we could see quite a good rally until the handover."
